<reason>PRO found the cleanest decision rule and held it: caps do the physical work, but a cap is a rationing device with no allocation rule, so the real question is "which 5,000?" CON's answer — lottery, open advance windows, FCFS — was pressed hard by PRO's Q1, and CON's reply (residents can enter "in March, in November, on a rainy Tuesday") was efficiently turned in PRO's closing: the motion is explicitly about peak season, so conceding residents the off-peak calendar concedes PRO's premise rather than rebutting it. CON never squarely repaired that. On the two objections CON needed, PRO gave direct, plausible answers: the residency line was closed with an ordinary municipal register generously written (resident/worker/student), with the sensible point that over-inclusion is cheap and fraud is deterred by tax liability — and CON's second rebuttal asserted this "never actually closed" without engaging the register. On revenue, PRO's Q2 ("name the euro") extracted CON's own admission that a city could reprice the tourist tier, after which CON pivoted to "then the carve-out is redistribution, not conservation" — a pivot PRO had already accepted openly, since its case was access, consent and cost-bearing, not conservation funding. CON's best material (fragility is about total footfall, not passports; residents' structural flexibility; the "border check on culture" framing) was genuinely sharp and kept the debate competitive, and PRO's consent argument went underused. But CON's closing overclaims that the carve-out drains conservation "by PRO's own math," which the exchange had already undercut, and it recycles the fragility framing PRO had conceded and absorbed in round one. PRO made the choice easier to decide; CON left the central allocation question answered only by a procedure it had itself described as off-peak.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's closing turn on CON's own answer: CON defended neutral rationing by noting residents can try "in March, in November, on a rainy Tuesday," and PRO showed that this is a concession, not a rebuttal, because the motion is specifically about peak season — recasting CON's "neutrality" as an openly defended peak-season exclusion of the people who fund and host the site.</best_rebuttal>
